lead: A camera records numbers from a sensor, not a picture. Scene energy, usually light, falls on a sensor, which gives an electrical signal; a digitizer turns that signal into integers. This chapter follows the chain: spectrum bands that carry scene information, sensor response to light, and single, line and array arrangements that build a two-dimensional image.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for where these images are used, and Chapter 1.3 for the eye as a reference sensor.

blocks.text: Imaging records energy that leaves a scene. Most of it is electromagnetic radiation, described by its wavelength λ, the distance between successive crests, measured in metres. Imaging bands are quoted in nm (10⁻⁹ m) or µm (10⁻⁶ m). The wavelength decides what the radiation interacts with, so each band reveals different material.

items: Visible: about 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red). Reflected sunlight or a lamp; ordinary photography.
X-ray: about 0.01 nm to 10 nm. Passes through soft tissue, blocked by bone and metal; medical and industrial inspection.
Ultraviolet: about 10 nm to 400 nm. Fluorescence and surface cracks.
Infrared: about 700 nm to 1 mm. Emitted heat and reflected near-infrared; night vision and thermal cameras.
Microwave and radio: 1 mm to metres. Radar, satellite imaging, and MRI radio pulses.

blocks.text: When radiation reaches an object, part is reflected, part absorbed and part transmitted. Reflectance ρ(λ) is the fraction reflected at wavelength λ, between 0 and 1. A leaf reflects green and absorbs red and blue, so it looks green. The sensor records the radiation leaving the scene: reflected source light plus any light the object emits.

blocks.where: E is the irradiance on the surface in W/m², P is the radiant power of a point source in W, and d is the source-to-surface distance in m. Doubling d quarters E, which is why a lamp-lit photo dims fast with distance.

blocks.text: A sensor converts incident radiation into an electrical signal. In silicon cameras (CCD and CMOS), a photon frees an electron, and electrons collect as charge proportional to the light on that element during exposure. Readout gives a voltage v, and v ≈ R·E·t, where v is output voltage in V, R is responsivity in V·m²/J, E is irradiance in W/m², and t is exposure time in s. Since 1 J = 1 W·s, R·E·t has units of volts. Doubling t doubles v until the element saturates; in darkness a small noise floor remains.

The sensor output is continuous in space and value. The digitizer, or ADC (analog-to-digital converter), does two jobs: sampling fixes the positions or instants at which the signal is read, and quantization rounds each reading to the nearest of a fixed set of integers. In an array camera the sensor element grid fixes the positions and the ADC quantizes. Sampling and quantization rules are in Chapter 1.6.

A pixel (picture element) is one sample on the image grid. Bit depth is the number of bits b stored per sample; the sample takes 2^b levels, from 0 to 2^b − 1, so 8 bits gives 256 levels and 12 bits gives 4096. A frame is one complete two-dimensional image captured at one instant; video is a sequence of frames, and frame rate is in frames per second (fps). A sensor element is not a display pixel: a line sensor may have 4096 elements while the screen has 1920 columns.

blocks.where: rows and columns are the image dimensions in pixels and b is the bit depth in bits per pixel. Divide by 8 for bytes.

blocks.text: A single sensing element measures one point, so a two-dimensional image needs relative motion. In the classic drum-scanner and laboratory stage setup the sensor stays fixed and the object moves on a stage:

items: Place the object on a stage and illuminate it.
Read the element once; that gives one pixel.
Step the stage along one axis and read again, building one image row.
Step the stage along the perpendicular axis and repeat until all rows are collected.

blocks.text: This single-sensor method is slow but cheap, and some syllabi call it the single-sensor arrangement. A line sensor is a row of elements, for example 4096 side by side: one exposure gives a whole image row, and as the scene moves past at constant speed, row after row is appended. That is a pushbroom scan, used in Earth-observation satellites, flatbed document scanners and web-inspection cameras. An array sensor is a two-dimensional grid, for example 1920 × 1080 elements; one exposure gives a full frame at one instant, as in phone and machine-vision cameras.

The choice follows the motion. Array sensors suit moving or momentary scenes; line and single sensors suit flat or steadily moving objects and give very high resolution along one axis. Sampling is uniform when points are equally spaced in both directions, the normal case, and nonuniform when spacing varies, for example a log-polar grid dense at the centre. Nonuniform grids complicate indexing, so most pipelines resample them to a uniform grid.

figure.caption: The worked example as one chain: a 4096-element, 12-bit line sensor scanning 3000 rows at 400 rows/s builds 12,288,000 pixels and 147,456,000 bits, which is 18,432,000 bytes. Notice the last two blocks: the same buffer is 18.432 MB in decimal units and 17.578 MiB in binary units, and the whole scan takes 7.5 s.

spec.title: Line sensor scan: worked example
spec.aria: A 4096-element, 12-bit line sensor scanning 3000 rows at 400 rows per second gives 12,288,000 pixels, then 147,456,000 bits, then 18,432,000 bytes, which is 18.432 MB or 17.578 MiB, and the scan takes 7.5 seconds.

examples.question: A line sensor has 4096 elements and 12 bits per pixel. It scans a page 3000 lines long, at 400 lines per second. Find the raw image size in bytes and in MB and MiB, and the scan time in seconds.
steps: Pixels = elements per line × number of lines = 4096 × 3000 = 12,288,000 pixels.
Bits = pixels × bits per pixel = 12,288,000 × 12 = 147,456,000 bits.
Scan time = lines ÷ line rate = 3000 ÷ 400 = 7.5 s.
Check on the data rate: 18,432,000 bytes ÷ 7.5 s = 2,457,600 bytes/s, about 2.46 MB/s.
examples.answer: The raw image is 12,288,000 pixels, that is 147,456,000 bits = 18,432,000 bytes (18.432 MB, 17.578 MiB), and the scan takes 7.5 s.
examples.check:
elements = 4096
lines = 3000
bits_per_pixel = 12
line_rate = 400

pixels = elements * lines
bits = pixels * bits_per_pixel
num_bytes = bits // 8
mib = num_bytes / 1048576
mb = num_bytes / 1e6
seconds = lines / line_rate
print(pixels)
print(bits)
print(num_bytes)
print(mib)
print(mb)
print(seconds)

traps: Sensor elements and display pixels are not the same count. A 4096-element line sensor can produce an image you show on a 1920-column screen; resampling changes the numbers.
A line sensor builds rows over time, so line time, stage speed or satellite swath are about scanning, not a single frame. An array sensor captures a frame at one instant.
Bits and bytes: 12 bits per pixel is 1.5 bytes per pixel, not 12 bytes. Divide by 8 exactly once, at the end.
MB and MiB differ. 18.432 MB is 18,432,000 bytes while 17.578 MiB is a different number for the same buffer; read which one is asked.
Illumination is the light falling on the scene; reflectance is the fraction the object sends back. A well-lit black cloth still looks dark because its reflectance is low.

quiz.q: Define pixel, bit depth and frame.
quiz.a: A pixel is one sample of the image on its grid. Bit depth is the number of bits stored per sample, giving 2^b levels from 0 to 2^b − 1. A frame is one complete two-dimensional image captured at one instant.

quiz.q: Name the three sensor arrangements used in image acquisition and one application of each.
quiz.a: Single sensor with moving stage (drum and laboratory stage scanners), line sensor with pushbroom motion (flatbed/document scanning, satellite scanning), and array sensor (phone and machine-vision cameras).

quiz.q: Why does a single sensing element need a moving stage to form an image?
quiz.a: One element measures only one point at one position, giving one pixel. A two-dimensional image needs a grid of measurements, so the element and the object must move relative to each other along two perpendicular axes, one pixel at a time.

quiz.q: Explain the difference between illumination and reflectance, with one example.
quiz.a: Illumination is the radiation falling on a scene from a source, measured as irradiance in W/m². Reflectance is the fraction of that radiation the object sends back at a given wavelength, between 0 and 1. White paper in dim light can reflect more than black paper in bright light; the sensor sees illumination multiplied by reflectance.

quiz.q: A line sensor has 2048 elements and 8 bits per pixel. It scans 500 lines at 250 lines per second. Find the image size in bytes and the scan time.
An 8-bit gray image has 1024 rows and 1024 columns. How many bytes does the raw array need, and how many 256-level values does one pixel take?
quiz.a: Bytes = 1024 × 1024 × 8 ÷ 8 = 1,048,576 bytes = 1 MiB. With b = 8 the pixel takes 2^8 = 256 levels, from 0 to 255.

quiz.q: A camera offers 8-bit and 12-bit modes. Why is the 12-bit image not automatically a better picture?
quiz.a: Bit depth sets how finely the voltage is quantized, not how much light is collected. If the sensor noise floor is larger than one 12-bit step, the extra levels record noise, not detail. Higher bit depth helps only when dynamic range and noise allow it, and it costs 50 percent more storage per pixel.

quiz.q: A satellite uses a pushbroom line sensor rather than an array sensor. Give two reasons.
quiz.a: A long line sensor gives far more elements across a wide swath than an array of the same cost, so ground resolution is higher. The satellite's forward motion supplies the second scanning direction free, so no shutter or large two-dimensional detector is needed, and each row is exposed at the same instant across the swath.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern acquisition has moved past the frame model: event cameras report per-pixel brightness changes as a stream of asynchronous events, and time-of-flight and LiDAR sensors return a depth value per pixel instead of a brightness value. Hyperspectral cameras capture hundreds of narrow bands, so each pixel becomes a spectrum rather than a number. Search next for event-based vision, time-of-flight cameras, and pushbroom hyperspectral imaging.
